questions.question: A girl on roller skates stands still, facing a brick wall. She gives the wall a hard shove with both hands, and the wall does not budge. What happens to the girl?
questions.answer: She rolls backward, away from the wall
choices: She rolls backward, away from the wall
She stays put, since a wall cannot push
She stays put, since the wall did not move
She rolls forward, carried by her own push
questions.context: As she pushes on the wall, the wall pushes back on her hands just as hard, at the same moment, and that push rolls her backward. A still, solid thing like a wall can push: whenever one object pushes on another, the second pushes back. Her own push is not stored up to carry her anywhere.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C has 6th graders identify the force pairs between interacting objects, and a skater pushing off a wall is the standard case showing that a still wall pushes back.

questions.question: A swimmer sweeps her arms backward through the water, stroke after stroke, and glides forward across the pool. What pushes her forward?
questions.answer: The water, pushing forward on her hands
choices: The water, pushing forward on her hands
The water, closing in behind her body
The force she stores up with each stroke
The air above, pressing on her back
questions.context: Her hands and arms push the water backward, and the water pushes them forward just as hard; that forward push from the water moves her along. A swimmer stores up no force, since a force lasts only while two things act on each other, and the air above her does not push her along.
questions.grade_note: A swimmer pushing water back and moving forward is a named example in the 6th-grade third-law line (curriculum map G6.P7, TEKS 6.7C).

questions.question: A spacecraft drifts far out in space, where there is no air at all. It fires its rocket engine, and hot gas blasts out of the back. What happens to the spacecraft?
questions.answer: It speeds up, pushed forward by the gas
choices: It speeds up, pushed forward by the gas
It stays put, with no air to push against
It slows down, held back by the gas
It drifts backward, along with the gas
questions.context: The engine pushes the gas out backward, and the gas pushes the rocket forward just as hard. A rocket never needs air to push against, and it works even better in empty space, where its exhaust escapes freely. A New York Times editorial mocked the rocket pioneer Robert Goddard on this point in 1920, and the paper printed a correction in July 1969, during the flight of Apollo 11.
questions.grade_note: A rocket's exhaust is a named 6th-grade third-law example (curriculum map G6.P7), and textbooks name the belief that a rocket pushes on the air as a common misconception.

questions.question: A girl blows up a balloon and pinches its neck shut, with the open end pointing at the floor. She lets go, and air streams out of the neck toward the floor. What does the balloon do, and why?
questions.answer: Shoots up, pushed by the air rushing out
choices: Shoots up, pushed by the air rushing out
Drops down, dragged by the air rushing out
Floats up, since the air inside is light
Stays put, since air is too light to push
questions.context: The stretched balloon squeezes its air out downward, and the air pushes the balloon upward just as hard, so the balloon shoots off the opposite way to the escaping air. Breath is not lighter than the room's air, so a blown-up balloon left alone does not float; a gas lighter than air, such as helium, is needed for that.
questions.grade_note: A balloon let go, or a balloon rocket, is the classic grade-school demonstration of action and reaction (TEKS 5.7B names the balloon rocket; TEKS 6.7C asks for force pairs).

questions.question: A bug flying over a highway smacks into the windshield of a speeding truck. The bug is squashed flat, while the truck rolls on as if nothing had happened. How hard does the bug push on the truck?
questions.answer: Just as hard as the truck pushes on it
choices: Just as hard as the truck pushes on it
Far more weakly than the truck pushes on it
A bit more weakly than the truck pushes on it
Not at all, since the bug is far too light
questions.context: Forces come in equal pairs, so in the crash the bug pushes on the truck exactly as hard as the truck pushes on the bug. The same-sized push changes the tiny, light bug's motion enormously and the heavy truck's hardly at all, which is why only the bug is squashed.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C teaches that a force pair is equal in size, and NGSS MS-PS2-1 applies the law to collisions, where students commonly believe the heavier object pushes harder.

questions.question: A batter swings, and the bat smacks a pitched baseball and sends it flying. The bat pushes on the ball, and the ball pushes back on the bat. Why do these two forces not cancel each other out?
questions.answer: Each one acts on a different object
choices: Each one acts on a different object
The bat pushes harder than the ball does
The ball pushes back a moment later
Forces pointing opposite ways never cancel
questions.context: The two pushes are equal, opposite and come at the same moment, but one acts on the ball and the other on the bat. Forces cancel only when they act on the same object, as two equal pulls on one rope do, so the bat's push sends the ball flying while the ball's push acts on the bat instead.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade third-law line (curriculum map G6.P7) ends on exactly this: the two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.

questions.question: Isaac Newton's third law says that forces always come in pairs. A carpenter's hammer strikes a nail and drives it down into a board. Which force is the partner of the hammer's push on the nail?
questions.answer: The nail's push up on the hammer
choices: The nail's push up on the hammer
The board's push up on the nail
The hand's push down on the hammer
Earth's pull down on the nail
questions.context: A force pair is always the same two objects acting on each other: the hammer pushes on the nail, so the nail pushes back on the hammer, equally hard and the opposite way. The board's push is another force on the nail itself, so it belongs to a different pair, between the nail and the board.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.7C asks 6th graders to identify the force pairs that come from interactions between objects.

questions.question: An apple drops from a branch, pulled down by Earth's gravity. The apple pulls on Earth too. Why does no one ever see Earth move up to meet a falling apple?
questions.answer: Earth is so massive it barely moves
choices: Earth is so massive it barely moves
The apple's pull on Earth is far weaker
The two pulls cancel each other out
Earth's spin holds it firmly in place
questions.context: The apple pulls Earth up exactly as hard as Earth pulls the apple down, but Earth's mass is vastly larger, so the same-sized pull moves Earth far too little to notice while the apple drops to the ground. The two pulls act on different objects, so they cannot cancel, and Earth's spin has nothing to do with it.
questions.grade_note: NGSS PS2.A states the third law for any pair of interacting objects, gravity included, and 5th grade has already taught that more mass means less change in motion (Florida SC.5.P.13.3).
